preview: An interview experience detailing the multi-round hiring process at JPMC, including an online coding assessment, a HireVue video interview, and the Code For Good hackathon.
content: JP Morgan Chase & Co. Interview Experience Prit Kanadiya TY B. Tech. Computer Engineering '25 About JP Morgan Chase & Co. was the first company to visit our campus for internships for 3rd-year students. They conducted hiring exclusively through the Code For Good event, providing students with an opportunity to apply for the Software Engineer Program (SEP). Eligibility Criteria ● Degrees: B.Tech./B.E./MCA ● Streams or Specializations: Computer Science/Information Science/ Information Technology/Electronics/ Electrical/Electronics and Telecommunications/ Instrumentation/ Electronics and Communications ● A well-rounded academic background with minimum aggregate 7 CGPA or 70 % and above. ● Backlogs – No current backlogs ● Education Gap – Not more than 1 year Round I : Online Coding Round In the first challenge, we had an online coding round on Hackerrank. We got an hour to solve three problems. While I can't remember the exact questions, they were primarily based on Strings, Arrays, Hashmaps, Trees etc. I managed to solve all three questions within 40 minutes. To prepare, I worked on around 70-80 questions from various topics, using resources like Neetcode 150. I recommend solving at least 100 questions through any platform covering diverse topics and data structures. This kind of practice really helps build up problem-solving skills and confidence for competitive programming challenges. Round II : Hirevue interview After completing the coding test on Hackerrank, the next step in the process was an online video interview through HireVue. This interview usually includes two non-technical questions, focusing more on your experiences and how you've dealt with challenges in projects. Questions typically touch on topics like career goals, accomplishments, and recent learning experiences. You're expected to share examples from your past projects and articulate your responses effectively within a two-minute time frame. If needed, you also have the option to redo your response once per question. During my interview, I talked about my involvement in the e-Yantra Robotics Competition and other relevant projects to showcase my achievements and lessons learned. Sharing real-life examples from my experiences helped me provide concrete and relatable responses to the interview questions. To prepare for the interview, I made use of the sample questions provided by HireVue. These questions gave me a good idea of what to expect during the interview. Additionally, I found that many similar questions are available online, which allowed me to prepare rough answers in advance. Given that online interviews often follow a standard format, there's a high likelihood that these questions may come up. So, having prepared responses beforehand can greatly boost your confidence and performance during the interview. It's also very important to be yourself during the interview. Don't make up stories, hypothetical situations, or use fake accents. Stick to real experiences and speak naturally. Round III : Code For Good Hackathon Six weeks after the interviews, we received an email regarding selections for the Code for Good event. A total of 11 students were chosen and the event was set to be held online on August 15th and 16th. In the days preceding the hackathon, we underwent a few sessions aimed at equipping us with the necessary tools and strategies for the competition. Just a day before the hackathon, we were assigned teams and gained access to a GitHub repository, setting the stage for collaboration. During this period, we utilized LinkedIn to connect with team members and held meetings to decide upon our preferred tech stack. Through open discussions about our strengths and weaknesses, we collectively opted for React and the Django framework. Our team comprised six members from colleges across India. The night before the hackathon, we had an icebreaker meeting. Here, we met our three mentors who interactively engaged with us, helping us feel at ease. To break the ice further, we played games, and each mentor shared insights into their work at the company, answering our queries about projects undertaken at JPMC. As part of the pre-event activities, we were tasked with creating a meme and sharing it on the Slack channel. Additionally, we finalized our team name, settling on "CodeRed." At 9 in the morning on day 1, representatives from various organizations presented their problem statements, providing insights into the challenges they faced. We had the opportunity to learn about the expectations for potential solutions from each of the four NGOs, each presenting two problem statements. The presentation phase is very important since the organizations will share the problems they face and their expectations here. After the presentations, a preferences form was rolled out, and we swiftly filled it out as the challenges would be allotted on a first-come-first-serve basis. Our team secured our top choice, Bhumi NGO, an organization dedicated to providing education through volunteering and donations. The problem statement from Bhumi revolved around developing a standardized solution to attract more donors and raise funds through events, as well as implementing an efficient mechanism to collect feedback from stakeholders. Following the selection, we engaged in a crucial Q&A session with the NGO. This phase was vital as it allowed us to grasp the specific pain points faced by the organization. Through this interaction, we identified two main challenges: Firstly, the lack of feedback from attendees and volunteers, and secondly, the need to enhance fundraising efforts through events. After the Q&A, we brainstormed ideas for about an hour. Subsequently, around noon, we presented our proposed solutions to our mentors, who provided valuable feedback. By 1 pm, we had a clear plan in place and divided the team into three for frontend and three for backend development. Recognizing our team's weaker proficiency in backend tasks, we prioritized backend tasks and closely tracked the backend development. To streamline our work despite the remote nature of the hackathon, we established project management protocols. One team member and I took charge of overseeing the entire project and GitHub repository, while everyone updated their progress regularly on a shared spreadsheet. The product we created featured two core components: Firstly, a gamified form accessible via a QR code at events, where users could provide feedback in a fun and engaging manner. Secondly, a badge system incentivizing donations, with badges shareable on social media platforms. Additionally, our solution included several other features such as event tracking, location management, and fundraising. During the hackathon, we had many brainstorming sessions to think up clever and easy solutions to the problems. For example, we noticed most volunteers were young, so we made sure our feedback system was appealing to them. Our mentors joined these sessions and watched how we worked together and what ideas we came up with. They also gave us feedback on our ideas. I think the main goal of the hackathon was to come up with new and creative ideas, rather than just putting them into action. Additionally, we had two one-on-one meetings with our mentors during the hackathon. They asked us about the problem statements, our contributions thus far, and other non-technical aspects. Following the coding cut-off at 10 AM, we were unable to make further commits to our GitHub repository. The mentors rejoined us to review our completed project, giving us one hour to finalize and submit our solutions. Knowing that our project would be evaluated in the technical judging round scheduled at 11:30 AM, we opted for a pre-recorded video presentation to showcase our work efficiently. Evaluation & Results During our first pitch at the hackathon, we confidently presented our project among 10 competing teams. The judges were impressed, and we happily found out we made it to the next round. During the break between rounds, my teammates and I took some time to relax and get to know each other better, chatting about our interests, schools, and past projects. Moving into the second round with two other teams, we stayed focused and presented our project again. Unlike some of the other teams, we didn't use AI or machine learning because we didn't think it was necessary for the NGO's problem. We kept things simple and only added features that directly solved the problem at hand. Before diving into fancy technology like AI and chatbots during hackathons, we must always ask ourselves if it's truly needed or if there's a simpler solution. While many other teams went for complex solutions with chatbots and advanced machine learning models, we stuck to a simpler approach that perfectly solved the NGO's problem. This ended up giving us an advantage in the competition. A few weeks later, we received our rewards, including some cool goodies and an iPad for our team's success. Internship Offer & Conclusion On August 25th, we received an email from the Training and Placement Office (TPO) confirming the selection of 6 students from the campus for the Software Engineer Program at J.P. Morgan Chase & Co.
